title: One Faithful Pass Over the Cuckoo's Nest
comment: Proceedings of the AISB Convention 2026, Jul 1-2, 2026, University of Sussex, Brighton, UK, Symposium: Is Consciousness a Story We Tell Ourselves?
summary: Narrative theories of consciousness hold that conscious experience is (at least partly) constituted by a partially opaque inner narrative that does not perfectly track the underlying computation it narrates. I argue that the safety goal of making chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning faithful and transparent is structurally incompatible with the conditions under which CoT could, even in principle, count as conscious narration. Recent empirical work suggests that CoT in large language models is largely post hoc, causally bypassed, and unreliable as a window onto internal computation. The opacity that makes CoT unreliable for alignment is exactly what narrative theories of consciousness identify as consciousness-constitutive. Alignment interventions aimed at producing faithful CoT and consciousness-detection frameworks grounded in narrative theory are therefore pulling the same architectural variable in opposite directions. I draw out the methodological consequence: alignment interventions alter the very features that consciousness-detection frameworks would need to measure, a point neither field has addressed directly.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that efforts to make chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs faithful and transparent—a key alignment goal—are structurally incompatible with narrative theories of consciousness, which hold that conscious experience requires a partially opaque inner narrative. Since CoT's unreliability as a window onto internal computation is precisely what would make it conscious under narrative theory, alignment interventions and consciousness-detection frameworks based on narrative theory pull the same architectural variable in opposite directions. This creates an unaddressed methodological conflict where alignment changes the very features consciousness detection would need to measure.
AI.motivation: To expose a fundamental tension between two AI research agendas—alignment efforts seeking faithful/transparent CoT and consciousness-detection frameworks grounded in narrative theory—which are structurally incompatible yet neither field has directly addressed this conflict.
AI.method: The paper develops a philosophical/analytical argument drawing on narrative theories of consciousness, applies them to empirical findings on CoT in LLMs (shown to be post hoc, causally bypassed, and unreliable), and derives the structural incompatibility between alignment's safety goals (faithful CoT) and the conditions under which CoT could constitute conscious narration (opacity).
AI.result: The analysis reveals that the opacity making CoT unreliable for alignment purposes is exactly what narrative theories identify as consciousness-constitutive, meaning alignment interventions and narrative-theory-based consciousness detection are pulling the same architectural variable in opposite directions, with methodological consequences for both fields that neither has addressed.
AI.conclusion: Alignment interventions change the very features that narrative-theory-based consciousness-detection frameworks would need to measure, creating an unaddressed methodological conflict between the goals of faithful CoT for safety and detectable conscious narration.

title: A distributed-delay Wilson-Cowan model of sleep-related rhythms in the corticothalamic system
summary:
The corticothalamic circuit supports rhythms with timescales that differ by orders of magnitude: sleep spindles, the sigma-band events of non-rapid-eye-movement (NREM) sleep, and infra-slow fluctuations near 0.02Hz that organize when spindles occur. Because the anatomy is the same in both cases, architecture alone cannot determine which rhythm the circuit expresses. We ask whether the temporal structure of the circuit's own feedback can. In a four-population Wilson--Cowan model comprising cortical excitatory and inhibitory populations, thalamic relay cells, and the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), we first establish how connectivity controls access to oscillatory behavior, and then introduce temporal coupling as either a weak Gamma distributed delay or a discrete delay.
  We investigate three distinct connectivity levels: recurrent cortical excitation gates whether the circuit can oscillate at all, the reciprocal relay-TRN pair determines where the oscillation lies and how it is configured, sustained, and terminated, and reticular self-inhibition limits its extent. We then examine how these connectivity-dependent regimes are affected by delayed coupling. Although delay does not change the equilibria themselves, it can substantially alter their stability and the organization of the resulting oscillatory dynamics. Under weak Gamma integration, short delays support spindle-compatible oscillations in the sigma band, while longer delays give rise to a much slower regime near 0.02Hz. The discrete-delay formulation produces a qualitatively different and more complex bifurcation structure. Together, these results show that the dynamics of the corticothalamic circuit depend not only on its connectivity, but also on the temporal organization of interactions within the circuit.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a four-population Wilson-Cowan model of the corticothalamic circuit to investigate how temporal feedback structure, rather than architecture alone, determines whether the circuit expresses sleep spindles (~sigma band) or infra-slow fluctuations (~0.02Hz). Connectivity controls oscillatory access and configuration, while the temporal organization of coupling (Gamma-distributed vs. discrete delays) selects between fast spindle-compatible and slow rhythms, without changing equilibria but fundamentally altering their stability and bifurcation structure.
AI.motivation: The corticothalamic circuit produces rhythms differing by orders of magnitude (sleep spindles vs. infra-slow fluctuations), yet uses identical anatomy in both cases. Since architecture alone cannot explain which rhythm is expressed, the authors ask whether the temporal structure of the circuit's own feedback determines the rhythm.
AI.method: A four-population Wilson-Cowan model is constructed with cortical excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations, thalamic relay cells, and the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN). Connectivity effects are first established without delays, then temporal coupling is introduced as either a weak Gamma-distributed delay or a discrete delay. Three connectivity levels are examined: recurrent cortical excitation (gating oscillation), reciprocal relay-TRN pair (determining oscillation location/configuration/sustainment/termination), and reticular self-inhibition (limiting extent).
AI.result: Short Gamma delays support spindle-compatible oscillations in the sigma band, while longer delays produce a much slower regime near 0.02Hz. The discrete-delay formulation yields a qualitatively different and more complex bifurcation structure. Delays do not change equilibria but can substantially alter their stability and the organization of oscillatory dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The dynamics of the corticothalamic circuit depend not only on connectivity but also on the temporal organization of interactions within the circuit—specifically, the temporal structure of feedback can determine which of the two rhythm regimes is expressed.

title: BME-like Quartet Weights for Phylogenetic Trees
comment: 31 pages. Lean 4 verification and table-reproduction materials are provided as ancillary files
summary: Like pairwise distances, quartets can be highly redundant and correlated on a phylogenetic tree, and their number grows on the order of n^4 rather than n^2. I explore BME-like weights for reweighting quartet scores before summing them to score a full tree. Three weights are considered on an unrooted binary tree: w_ext(q)=2^(-I_ext(q)), w_int(q)=2^(-I_int(q)), and w_tot(q)=2^(-I_tot(q))=w_ext(q)w_int(q), where the exponents count specified internal nodes in the minimal connecting subtree of a quartet. Exact tree-shape counts, total quartet-weight sums, and internal-edge crossing sums are calculated for all unlabeled unrooted binary tree shapes on 6-10 taxa. For w_ext, the total quartet weight is tree-shape-invariant and the edge-crossing sum depends only on split size. For any n-leaf tree, we prove sum_q w_ext(q)=(n-2)(n-3)/8, and the sum over quartets crossing an internal edge with split a|b equals (a-1)(b-1)/4. Exact tree-shape-specific normalizers are also derived for w_int and w_tot. A degree-corrected hard-polytomy extension is given for multifurcating trees, and a conditional consistency result shows that these positive weights preserve consistency when the underlying quartet estimates are themselves consistent for the true induced quartet states. These results provide a mathematical foundation for evaluating and applying BME-like quartet weights to reduce redundancy with the particular aim of improving statistical efficiency with finite data.

AI.tldr: This paper explores Balanced Minimal Evolution (BME)-like weighting schemes for quartets on phylogenetic trees, analyzing three weight functions (w_ext, w_int, w_tot) defined by counts of specified internal nodes in quartets' minimal connecting subtrees. Exact combinatorial calculations for trees with 6-10 taxa show w_ext has tree-shape-invariant properties with proven closed-form sums, while w_int and w_tot require tree-shape-specific normalizers. The work includes extensions to multifurcating trees and a conditional consistency result, providing mathematical foundations for improving statistical efficiency of quartet-based phylogenetic inference.
AI.motivation: Quartets on phylogenetic trees are highly redundant and correlated (growing as O(n^4)), and naive summation of quartet scores leads to redundancy that may reduce statistical efficiency with finite data. The paper seeks mathematically grounded weighting schemes—analogous to BME weighting for pairwise distances—to reduce this redundancy and improve inference.
AI.method: The authors define three quartet weight functions based on the counts of specified internal nodes in the minimal connecting subtree: w_ext(q)=2^(-I_ext(q)), w_int(q)=2^(-I_int(q)), and w_tot(q)=w_ext(q)w_int(q). They perform exact enumerations over all unlabeled unrooted binary tree shapes on 6-10 taxa, computing tree-shape counts, total quartet-weight sums, and internal-edge crossing sums. They prove closed-form formulas for w_ext (total weight and edge-crossing sum are shape-invariant) and derive tree-shape-specific normalizers for w_int and w_tot. A degree-corrected hard-polytomy extension handles multifurcating trees, and a conditional consistency theorem establishes that the positive weights preserve consistency when quartet estimates are themselves consistent.
AI.result: For w_ext, the total quartet weight is proven to be (n-2)(n-3)/8 regardless of tree shape, and the sum over quartets crossing an internal edge with split a|b is (a-1)(b-1)/4, depending only on split size. Exact tree-shape-specific normalizers are derived for w_int and w_tot via enumeration on 6-10 taxa. The multifurcating extension and consistency preservation guarantee provide theoretical guarantees for practical use.
AI.conclusion: These results establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for BME-like quartet weighting schemes, offering principled approaches to reduce quartet redundancy with the aim of improving statistical efficiency in finite-data phylogenetic inference.

title: Operationalizing open-ended biological discovery across single-cell representations
summary: Single-cell studies are typically initiated from predefined research questions, leaving much of the biological information encoded within existing data unexplored. We formalize open-ended discovery as an analytical paradigm, in which data-derived signals are identified before biological context is interrogated and subsequently evaluated according to their potential to justify prospective experimental investment. Here we develop PROSPECTor, an end-to-end framework that searches for reproducible biological structures across conventional expression representations and diverse foundation-model embeddings, translating robust signals into quantitatively testable candidate hypotheses. Projection into unseen datasets then evaluates their generalizability and phenotype association, providing a scalable screen for candidates that warrant prospective validation. Supported signals emerged from different representation spaces and search strategies. PROSPECTor-nominated hypotheses were then examined in independent biological settings: fibroblast extracellular-matrix programmes demonstrated transferability to an independent mouse cohort with an intervention context, while a patient-resolved gastric-cancer T-cell programme recurred across single-cell, bulk and spatial cohorts. PROSPECTor establishes an auditable framework for systematically revisiting single-cell datasets across expanding representation spaces, turning retrospective collections into prospective resources for biological discovery that can motivate new research questions.

AI.tldr: PROSPECTor is an end-to-end framework for open-ended discovery in single-cell data that searches for reproducible biological structures across multiple representation spaces (conventional and foundation-model embeddings), evaluates their generalizability in unseen datasets, and translates robust signals into testable hypotheses for prospective validation.
AI.motivation: Single-cell studies are traditionally hypothesis-driven from predefined research questions, leaving biological information in existing datasets unexplored. There is a need to formalize open-ended discovery where data-derived signals are identified before biological context is interrogated, enabling systematic reuse of retrospective data.
AI.method: PROSPECTor searches for reproducible biological structures across both conventional expression representations and diverse foundation-model embeddings. It translates robust signals into quantitatively testable hypotheses, then projects them into unseen datasets to evaluate generalizability and phenotype association, serving as a scalable screen for candidate hypotheses warranting prospective validation.
AI.result: The framework identified supported signals from different representation spaces and search strategies. PROSPECTor-nominated hypotheses were validated in independent settings: fibroblast extracellular-matrix programmes transferred to an independent mouse cohort with an intervention context, and a patient-resolved gastric-cancer T-cell programme recurred across single-cell, bulk, and spatial cohorts.
AI.conclusion: PROSPECTor establishes an auditable framework for systematically revisiting single-cell datasets across expanding representation spaces, converting retrospective collections into prospective resources that can motivate new research questions and guide experimental investment.

title: Efficiently classifying shocks in complex systems requires dormant reporters
summary: Many natural and engineered systems are large complex networks of interacting components, and external perturbations drive them along different dynamical paths. Identifying which perturbation occurred matters for diagnosis, control, and prediction. Yet often times only a few components can be jointly monitored. Which components should be monitored? Experimental practice usually favors placing reporters at the most sensitive sites, where perturbations produce the largest effects. Using a simple dynamical model for complex systems with heterogeneous connectivity, we ask how sparse reporter panels should be chosen to classify shocks from partial trajectories when repeated trials only approximately reproduce an ideal initial condition. Once that reproduction is imperfect, sensitivity ranked panels fall far short of optimal, and the shortfall grows with the noise. We find that the best panels mix two kinds of reporters. A promiscuous reporter responds to most shocks, so it separates them mainly by degree, and degree fluctuates from trial to trial. A dormant reporter responds to only a few shocks but strongly, and its answers do not scatter as much between trials. As noise grows, the cost of losing a dormant reporter rises to meet the cost of losing a promiscuous one. Panels of either kind alone classify worse than the mixture, and no property of the members collected individually explains the ordering. Most of all, we find that only a minuscule number of reporters are needed on a panel to accurately identify which shock hit the system. We implement an efficient algorithm to assemble such a panel. Together these results provide a low cost practical design principle for monitoring large complex dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to select sparse reporter panels to classify external perturbations (shocks) in complex dynamical networks when monitoring is limited and initial conditions are only approximately reproducible. Sensitivity-ranked panels underperform under noise; optimal panels mix "promiscuous" reporters (respond to most shocks) with "dormant" reporters (respond strongly to only a few shocks), and only a tiny number of reporters are needed for accurate shock identification.
AI.motivation: Identifying which perturbation occurred in large complex networks matters for diagnosis, control, and prediction, but only few components can be monitored. The practical question is which components should be chosen for monitoring panels, especially when repeated trials only approximately reproduce ideal initial conditions—a realistic constraint not typically addressed.
AI.method: Using a simple dynamical model for complex systems with heterogeneous connectivity, the authors analyze how sparse reporter panels should be chosen to classify shocks from partial trajectories under imperfect initial condition reproduction. They introduce an efficient algorithm to assemble optimal panels, comparing sensitivity-ranked selection against mixture panels of promiscuous and dormant reporters.
AI.result: Sensitivity-ranked panels fall far short of optimal when initial condition reproduction is imperfect, and the shortfall grows with noise. Optimal panels mix promiscuous and dormant reporters: promiscuous reporters separate shocks by degree (which fluctuates between trials), while dormant reporters respond strongly to few shocks with less trial-to-trial scatter. As noise grows, the cost of losing a dormant reporter rises to match that of losing a promiscuous one. Panels of either kind alone underperform the mixture, and only a minuscule number of reporters is needed for accurate classification.
AI.conclusion: Only a very small number of reporters is needed to accurately identify shocks, and a practical design principle emerges: mix both promiscuous and dormant reporters in monitoring panels. The efficient algorithm provides a low-cost approach for real-world monitoring of large complex dynamical systems.

title: Temporally constraining source imaging estimates in an underdetermined neural system with eigenmodes of cortical geometry
summary: Geometric eigenmodes provide a compact and biologically grounded representation of large-scale neural activity. Previous work demonstrated that they can mitigate the underdetermined nature of electroencephalographic (EEG) and magnetoencephalographic (MEG) source localisation, an ill-posed inverse problem in which neural activity is reconstructed from non-invasive recordings. Beyond their spatial structure, neural field theory predicts the temporal evolution of eigenmodes through analytically derived transfer functions. Motivated by this framework, the present work investigates whether these transfer functions can be used to introduce temporal constraints into EEG source imaging. The approach is evaluated using simulated seizure dynamics generated by coupled Epileptor neural mass models. Transfer functions derived directly from neural field theory were found to be generally ineffective as temporal constraints for source localisation, primarily because they neglect cross-eigenmode coupling. Incorporating empirically estimated coupling terms substantially improves localisation performance, particularly in noisy conditions. Although estimating these eigenmode coupling interactions from experimental data remains challenging, the findings motivate dynamical source-imaging approaches that combine spatial eigenmode structure with empirically informed cross-modal dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether neural field theory-derived transfer functions can serve as temporal constraints for EEG source imaging. The authors found that transfer functions derived purely from theory are ineffective because they neglect cross-eigenmode coupling, but incorporating empirically estimated coupling terms substantially improves localization performance, especially under noisy conditions.
AI.motivation: Geometric eigenmodes offer a compact and biologically grounded representation of neural activity and can address the underdetermined nature of EEG/MEG source localization. Since neural field theory predicts temporal evolution of eigenmodes via analytically derived transfer functions, the authors explore whether these transfer functions can introduce temporal constraints into EEG source imaging, potentially improving the ill-posed inverse problem.
AI.method: The approach evaluates neural field theory transfer functions as temporal constraints for EEG source imaging using simulated seizure dynamics generated by coupled Epileptor neural mass models. Performance is compared between purely theoretical transfer functions and those augmented with empirically estimated coupling terms, particularly under varying noise conditions.
AI.result: Pure theoretical transfer functions were generally ineffective as temporal constraints for source localization because they neglect cross-eigenmode coupling. However, incorporating empirically estimated coupling terms substantially improved localization performance, especially in noisy conditions. Estimating eigenmode coupling from experimental data remains challenging.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate dynamical source-imaging approaches that combine spatial eigenmode structure with empirically informed cross-modal dynamics, suggesting that pure theory-based temporal constraints are insufficient and empirical coupling estimation is needed for practical improvement.

title: Active Visual Semantics: A large-scale MEG and eye-tracking dataset for understanding visual intelligence in action
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. High-resolution figures are provided at the end of the manuscript PDF. M.N. Hebart and T.C. Kietzmann contributed equally. Corresponding authors: P. Sulewski (phsulewski@gmail.com), T.C. Kietzmann (tim.kietzmann@uni-osnabrueck.de)
summary: Here we present the Active Visual Semantics (AVS) dataset, a large-scale collection of magnetoencephalography (MEG) and eye-tracking data recorded while five participants freely explored 4,080 natural scenes over 10 sessions each, yielding more than 200,000 fixation epochs in total. Unlike existing neuroimaging datasets that rely on passive viewing with enforced central fixation, AVS captures brain activity during active scene exploration, including self-generated saccades and fixations. A semantic captioning task on 25% of the trials provides behavioural measures linking gaze to scene understanding and memory. In addition to neural and behavioural data, AVS includes per-fixation object category labels, human-rated annotations of the appearance of fixation targets in the scene captioning task and pupil dynamics. Individual head stabilisation casts were used during MEG data collection, which alongside with structural MRI scans, enabled precise cross-session source reconstruction. Using artificial neural network (ANN) encoding models we demonstrate that individual fixation-aligned MEG epochs hold visual content-specific signal, despite the challenges that active scene viewing poses for MEG signal quality. Further, we use fixation-aligned representation similarity analysis (RSA) and demonstrate that we can derive fixation object category averages that yield representational geometries which are highly reliable across participants. Both in MEG sensor and source space this structure is validated by its robust alignment with ANN object-level representational geometry. Taken together, AVS provides a rich resource for investigating a large variety of questions regarding the neural mechanisms of active vision, object recognition and scene captioning during natural viewing, and the relationship between gaze behaviour and memory encoding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AVS (Active Visual Semantics), a large-scale MEG and eye-tracking dataset (5 participants, 4,080 natural scenes, 200,000+ fixation epochs) recorded during active scene exploration rather than passive viewing. It includes semantic captions, object labels, pupil dynamics, and head-stabilized MEG with MRI-based source reconstruction. ANN encoding models and RSA analyses demonstrate that fixation-aligned MEG epochs contain content-specific and cross-participant reliable neural signals.
AI.motivation: Existing neuroimaging datasets rely on passive viewing with enforced central fixation, failing to capture brain activity during natural, active scene exploration where self-generated eye movements occur.
AI.method: Collected MEG and eye-tracking data from 5 participants freely exploring 4,080 natural scenes across 10 sessions each. Used head stabilization casts and structural MRI for source reconstruction. Applied ANN encoding models and fixation-aligned representation similarity analysis (RSA) to validate neural signals.
AI.result: Fixation-aligned MEG epochs contain visual content-specific signal despite challenges of active viewing; RSA-derived fixation object category averages yield representational geometries that are highly reliable across participants and align with ANN object-level representations in both sensor and source space.
AI.conclusion: AVS provides a rich resource for investigating neural mechanisms of active vision, object recognition, scene captioning during natural viewing, and gaze-behavior-memory relationships.

title: From static structures to dynamic landscapes: cryo-EM redefines RNA biology
summary: RNA molecules perform diverse biological functions by dynamically exploring multiple conformational states rather than adopting a single static structure. Capturing these ensembles is a challenge in molecular biology. Recent advances in cryoEM are now transforming this landscape by enabling the visualization of RNA molecules across a broad spectrum of functionally relevant conformations at near atomic resolution. Here, we examine how cryoEM is reshaping RNA structural biology changing focus from the analysis of static structures to dynamic conformational landscapes. Through 8 representative case studies we illustrate how cryoEM has revealed previously inaccessible mechanisms of RNA motion, including folding processes, ligand-dependent switching, and cooperative assembly. We specifically discuss emerging experimental and computational approaches that address and overcome the challenges associated with studying dynamic RNAs, particularly in construct design, sample preparation, vitrification, and data analysis. These novel methods resolve conformational variability and enable the reconstruction of discrete and continuous RNA conformational landscapes from cryoEM data, highlighting how structural heterogeneity can be harnessed to extract functional insights. Looking forward, the integration of cryoEM with complementary biophysical techniques and time resolved methodologies promises to bridge structural and temporal resolution, to routinely derive experimental molecular movies of RNA in action. These advances will not only deepen our understanding of RNA biology but also provide new opportunities for RNA targeted therapeutics and the rational design of dynamic RNA-based nanodevices. By connecting structural snapshots into coherent dynamic models, cryoEM is establishing a framework for quantitative descriptions of RNA energy landscapes and their functional roles.

AI.tldr: This review examines how cryoEM is transforming RNA structural biology from static structure determination to capturing dynamic conformational landscapes, using 8 case studies illustrating folding, ligand-dependent switching, and cooperative assembly, while discussing emerging methods to overcome challenges in construct design, sample preparation, vitrification, and data analysis for reconstructing discrete and continuous conformational ensembles.
AI.motivation: RNA molecules function through dynamic conformational ensembles rather than static structures, yet capturing these dynamic states has been a major challenge in molecular biology. The paper addresses the need to shift from static structural analysis toward understanding RNA conformational landscapes and their functional implications.
AI.method: The paper presents a review approach: (1) analyzing 8 representative case studies demonstrating how cryoEM reveals RNA motion mechanisms including folding, ligand-dependent switching, and cooperative assembly; (2) discussing experimental and computational strategies to overcome challenges in construct design, sample preparation, vitrification, and data analysis; (3) examining methods for resolving conformational variability and reconstructing discrete and continuous RNA conformational landscapes from cryoEM data.
AI.result: CryoEM has enabled visualization of RNA across functionally relevant conformations at near-atomic resolution, revealing previously inaccessible dynamic mechanisms. Novel methods now allow reconstruction of discrete and continuous RNA conformational landscapes, and structural heterogeneity can be harnessed to extract functional insights from cryoEM data.
AI.conclusion: The integration of cryoEM with complementary biophysical techniques and time-resolved methodologies promises to bridge structural and temporal resolution, enabling routine derivation of experimental molecular movies of RNA in action. This will deepen understanding of RNA biology, support RNA-targeted therapeutics and dynamic RNA-based nanodevice design, and establish frameworks for quantitative descriptions of RNA energy landscapes.

title: On the interpretation of the kinetics of ligand-receptor binding
comment: 39 pages, 7 in-text figures, electronic supplementary material available: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.33406285
summary: When the rates of ligand binding are measured by methods such as surface plasmon resonance, it is common practice to use the observed rate constants for the onset and offset of binding to estimate an equilibrium constant for ligand binding. If this agrees with the equilibrium constant found as the EC50 for binding at equilibrium, this is taken as validation of the measured rates. This is correct only when binding produces no conformation change in the receptor, and ligand binding follows a single exponential time course. Here, we investigate a simple 3 state model in which binding is followed by a conformation change in the receptor. Three special cases of this model in which the time course of onset and offset of ligand binding are close to being single exponentials are analysed. These cases are (1) when binding is much faster than the conformation change, (2) when the conformation change is much faster than binding, and (3) when the rates of ligand dissociation and receptor activation are both fast. It is concluded that the measured rates will often yield an estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding that is close to the effective, or macroscopic, equilibrium constant, the EC50 found by measuring binding at equilibrium, which depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants describing ligand binding and the conformation change. The exception to this conclusion is the case when binding is much faster than the subsequent conformation change, though the estimate of the equilibrium constant for ligand binding still depends on both of the underlying microscopic equilibrium constants.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a 3-state model where ligand binding is followed by a receptor conformation change, examining whether rate constants measured by methods like SPR can reliably estimate equilibrium constants for ligand binding.
AI.motivation: Common practice assumes that the ratio of measured association and dissociation rate constants gives a valid equilibrium constant if it matches the EC50 from equilibrium binding experiments. However, this validation is only correct when binding produces no conformational change in the receptor and follows a single exponential time course, so the authors investigate when this assumption fails.
AI.method: The authors analyze a simple 3-state kinetic model (ligand binding followed by receptor conformation change) and examine three special cases where the time courses of binding onset and offset are approximately single exponentials: (1) binding much faster than conformation change, (2) conformation change much faster than binding, and (3) both ligand dissociation and receptor activation being fast.
AI.result: The measured rates typically yield an equilibrium constant estimate close to the effective (macroscopic) equilibrium constant—the EC50 from equilibrium binding—which depends on both microscopic equilibrium constants (for ligand binding and conformation change). The exception is when binding is much faster than the subsequent conformation change, though even then the estimated equilibrium constant still depends on both underlying microscopic equilibrium constants.
AI.conclusion: The standard validation approach for kinetic rate measurements generally works in most circumstances even when conformational changes occur, but it can be misleading when ligand binding is much faster than the conformational change, since the "equilibrium constant" derived from rates reflects both binding and conformational equilibria rather than just the intrinsic binding step.

title: PopPert: Population-level Joint-Distribution Modeling for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Predicting transcriptional responses to specific perturbations is critical for understanding cellular regulatory mechanisms and accelerating drug discovery. Single-cell RNA sequencing destroys each measured cell, yielding only unpaired populations of control and perturbed cells. However, existing methods typically model perturbation prediction at the single-cell level and assume cell-to-cell correspondence, which conflicts with the unpaired nature of the observed data. To address this challenge, we propose PopPert, a framework that explicitly parameterizes population-level joint gene expression distributions for collective transcriptional state modeling. Given a control population distribution and a perturbation condition, PopPert predicts perturbation-induced changes in distribution parameters, eliminating the need for cell-level correspondence and reducing sensitivity to single-cell noise. To effectively capture gene co-expression patterns, PopPert leverages a low-rank Gaussian Copula to model cross-gene statistical dependencies and construct the joint gene expression distribution, additionally allowing sampling of synthetic perturbed single-cell profiles. Across multiple single-cell benchmarks spanning both genetic and chemical perturbations, PopPert achieves superior overall performance in differential expression recovery, perturbation effect estimation, and population-level distribution matching. These results establish population-level joint distribution learning as an effective paradigm for predicting transcriptional responses from unpaired single-cell populations. Code for PopPert is publicly available at https://github.com/whd1125/PopPert.

AI.tldr: PopPert is a framework that predicts transcriptional responses to perturbations by modeling population-level joint gene expression distributions using a low-rank Gaussian Copula, avoiding the need for cell-to-cell correspondence that conflicts with the unpaired nature of scRNA-seq data.
AI.motivation: Existing perturbation prediction methods operate at the single-cell level and assume cell-to-cell correspondence, but scRNA-seq destroys cells during measurement, yielding only unpaired populations of control and perturbed cells. This mismatch between assumptions and observed data limits accuracy and robustness.
AI.method: PopPert explicitly parameterizes population-level joint gene expression distributions. Given a control population distribution and a perturbation condition, it predicts changes in distribution parameters. It leverages a low-rank Gaussian Copula to capture cross-gene statistical dependencies and construct joint distributions, enabling sampling of synthetic perturbed single-cell profiles.
AI.result: Across multiple single-cell benchmarks covering both genetic and chemical perturbations, PopPert achieves superior performance in differential expression recovery, perturbation effect estimation, and population-level distribution matching compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Population-level joint distribution learning is an effective paradigm for predicting transcriptional responses from unpaired single-cell populations, and PopPert's public code enables further adoption.

title: Learning Task-Specific Antibody Representations via Function-Aware Masking
summary: Antibody-specific language models pretrained via masked language modeling (MLM) learn representations that are critical for downstream sequence design and property prediction tasks. Yet, the corruption process itself is rarely leveraged as a source of inductive bias during pretraining. While preferentially masking complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) improves binding-related predictions, antibodies possess diverse biological priors over a variety of functions. Herein, we introduce function-aware masking, a family of pretraining algorithms that align mask placement with specific functional priors (e.g., from IMGT annotations or structure predictions) to shape the learned representation space. We show that these specialist masking strategies significantly improve performance on their respective objectives, yielding up to a 14% gain on structure-related tasks and up to a 5.9x improvement on CDR-related tasks. To further improve performance across multiple functional axes, we develop hybrid masking strategies that integrate multiple priors, balancing reconstruction over binding, structural, and biophysical objectives. Our results demonstrate that informed mask placement provides a parameter-free mechanism for imposing functional inductive biases in antibody language model training.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "function-aware masking," a family of pretraining algorithms for antibody language models that align mask placement with specific functional priors (e.g., IMGT annotations or structural predictions) to shape learned representations. These specialist masking strategies improve performance on respective objectives, and hybrid strategies integrating multiple priors balance reconstruction across binding, structural, and biophysical tasks, providing a parameter-free mechanism for imposing functional inductive biases.
AI.motivation: While antibody-specific language models pretrained via masked language modeling learn useful representations, the corruption process itself is rarely leveraged as a source of inductive bias. Preferentially masking CDRs improves binding predictions, but antibodies have diverse biological priors across many functions, which current approaches do not fully exploit.
AI.method: The authors propose "function-aware masking," a family of pretraining algorithms that condition mask placement on specific functional priors (e.g., IMGT annotations or structure predictions) to shape the learned representation space. They also develop hybrid masking strategies that integrate multiple priors to balance reconstruction over binding, structural, and biophysical objectives.
AI.result: Specialist masking strategies significantly improve performance on their respective objectives, with up to a 14% gain on structure-related tasks and up to a 5.9x improvement on CDR-related tasks, demonstrating that informed mask placement provides a parameter-free approach for imposing functional inductive biases.
AI.conclusion: Function-aware masking offers an effective, parameter-free mechanism to embed functional inductive biases into antibody language model training, improving performance across multiple functional objectives without requiring additional model parameters.

title: Importance and methods to control, vary, and characterize mud strength for studying locomotion
comment: Journal of Experimental Biology, in review
summary: Animals and robots encounter mud at the water-land interface. Like sand, mud can stay solid or flow like a fluid. Unlike sand, the yield strength of mud at which solid-fluid transitions occur depends on not only the amount of solid relative to fluid (water in mud, air in dry sand), but also how much coarse grains and fine clay are within the solid. Despite understanding of locomotion on/within dry sand dominated by coarse grains with repulsive normal forces and friction, little is known for mud dominated by fine clay with strong cohesion. Here, we developed methods to prepare uniform mud of controlled, variable yield strength and characterize and track its drift from water evaporation. Compared to other flowable substrates, mud strength measured by upward force during penetration is weaker and can vary more, and mud sticks more during extraction to pull downward, making it more challenging for locomotion.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates locomotion in mud at the water-land interface, which differs fundamentally from locomotion in sand due to the cohesive nature of fine clay particles. The authors developed methods to prepare uniform mud with controlled yield strength and characterized how mud's strength and stickiness during extraction make locomotion more challenging than in other flowable substrates.
AI.motivation: Animals and robots commonly encounter mud at water-land interfaces, yet locomotion in mud is poorly understood compared to sand. Unlike dry sand (dominated by repulsive forces and friction in coarse grains), mud is dominated by fine clay with strong cohesion, and its yield strength depends on complex factors including solid content, coarse grain fraction, and clay fraction. This gap in understanding motivates the need for systematic study.
AI.method: The authors developed methods to prepare uniform mud samples with controlled, variable yield strength. They characterized and tracked mud drift caused by water evaporation, and measured mud strength during penetration (upward force) and extraction (downward pulling force) to compare against other flowable substrates.
AI.result: Compared to other flowable substrates, mud exhibits weaker and more variable strength when measured by upward force during penetration. Additionally, mud demonstrates greater stickiness during extraction, pulling downward, which presents added difficulty for locomotion.
AI.conclusion: Mud presents unique and more challenging conditions for locomotion than sand or other flowable substrates due to its weaker, more variable penetration strength and its tendency to stick and pull downward during extraction—challenges attributed to the cohesive properties of fine clay particles.

title: Mudskippers use tail thrusting to help crutching to move on mud of various wetness
comment: Journal of Experimental Biology, in review
summary: At the water-land interface, amphibious fishes encounter wet flowable substrates made of granular solid-water mixtures, which can stay solid or flow like a fluid. As these substrates become wetter or drier, their yield strength (at which solid-fluid transition occurs) and cohesion (how sticky they are) both change, challenging locomotion. Despite substantial understanding of tetrapod locomotion on flowable substrates (mostly dry sand), we know little about how amphibious fishes cope with wet flowable substrates of various wetness. Here, we studied mudskippers on clay mud of controlled, variable wetness over the range where solid-fluid transition occurs. As mud became wetter, its strength decreased by 100-fold, leading the animal to sink deeper, with larger areas of body and fins contacting mud. By contrast, mud stuck most easily at intermediate wetness. The increased sinkage and contact and stickiness change caused more mud to stick to and pull against the animal on wetter mud. We also tested dry mud, which stuck to animal fins as its mucus dried. Despite these challenges, the mudskipper predominately used a conserved crutching gait on all except the wettest mud tested, with a modest performance reduction. When normal crutching became less effective, the animal assisted it with tail thrusting, by bending and straightening it to push downward and backward to generate additional thrust and lift, or even thrusting the tail to jump. These observations suggest that mudskipper's crutching motor program is well adapted to its native muddy substrates but inflexible, with most novelty in tail use.

AI.tldr: This study examines how mudskippers, amphibious fishes, navigate wet flowable substrates of varying wetness at the water-land interface. Despite a 100-fold decrease in mud strength with increasing wetness causing deeper sinking and greater body contact, and maximum stickiness at intermediate wetness, mudskippers predominantly maintain a conserved crutching gait across conditions with modest performance reduction. When this gait fails on the wettest mud, they innovate by using tail thrusting and jumping for additional propulsion.
AI.motivation: Amphibious fishes face wet flowable substrates (granular solid-water mixtures) whose yield strength and cohesion change dramatically with wetness, yet little is known about how they cope—prior work has focused on tetrapod locomotion on dry sand rather than amphibious fish on wet variable substrates.
AI.method: The researchers studied mudskippers on clay mud with controlled, variable wetness spanning the solid-fluid transition range, measuring substrate strength, animal sinking depth, body/fin contact area, mud stickiness, and resulting locomotion performance (sinkage, mud adhesion, gait use).
AI.result: Wetter mud reduced strength 100-fold causing deeper sinking and larger contact areas, while stickiness peaked at intermediate wetness. Mud stuck to the animal and pulled against it more on wetter mud, and dry mud stuck to fins as mucus dried. Despite this, mudskippers used a conserved crutching gait on all but the wettest mud with modest performance loss, resorting to tail thrusting and jumps when crutching was ineffective.
AI.conclusion: The mudskipper's crutching motor program is well-adapted to its native muddy substrates but relatively inflexible, with behavioral novelty concentrated in tail use—suggesting that amphibious locomotion adaptation is conserved in body mechanics but flexible in appendage innovation.

title: FLaG: Frequency-Domain Latent-attention Gated Pooling for Token Aggregation
summary: Token aggregation converts token-level representations into fixed-dimensional sample representations, but most pooling methods operate only in the original token space. We introduce Frequency-Domain Latent-attention Gated Pooling (FLaG), a plug-in aggregation module that re-expresses encoder outputs in the Fourier domain before final pooling. FLaG represents the nonredundant rFFT spectrum through concatenated real and imaginary components, summarizes spectral tokens with learnable latent queries, derives a sample-conditioned channel gate, and reconstructs modulated token representations for downstream aggregation. We evaluate the same architecture across ESM2-based antimicrobial peptide (AMP) activity prediction, ResNet18 image classification on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and three RoBERTa-based language tasks. FLaG achieves the best macro-averaged Spearman correlation coefficient, RMSE, and Recall@50 across four AMP backbone-species settings and the highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR 10. It also achieves the best mean results on five of seven language metrics, although mean pooling remains strongest on STSBenchmark. AMP-side mechanistic analyses reveal low-frequency prediction sensitivity across most encoder layers, with increased relative high-frequency sensitivity in the final layer, and pronounced peptide-specific positional responses. The residual gate broadly amplifies spectral channels while preserving the low-frequency-dominated energy profile, whereas latent cross-attention exhibits sample- and species-specific spectral allocation. Overall, FLaG provides a transferable frequency-domain aggregation bias across protein, visual, and textual representations, with benefits that depend on the backbone and downstream task. Supplementary materials, source code, and data are available at https://www.healthinformaticslab.org/supp/ and https://github.com/Kewei2023/AMPCliff/tree/FLaG.

AI.tldr: FLaG is a plug-in aggregation module that re-expresses encoder outputs in the Fourier domain before final pooling, using rFFT spectra with learnable latent queries and sample-conditioned gating. It outperforms baselines on AMP activity prediction, CIFAR-10 image classification, and several RoBERTa-based language tasks, providing a transferable frequency-domain aggregation bias across protein, vision, and text domains.
AI.motivation: Token aggregation methods typically operate only in the original token space, limiting the representational capacity of pooling. The authors propose that re-expressing token representations in the frequency domain before aggregation could provide a more effective and transferable pooling strategy across diverse domains.
AI.method: FLaG represents the nonredundant real FFT (rFFT) spectrum via concatenated real and imaginary components, summarizes spectral tokens with learnable latent queries, derives a sample-conditioned channel gate, and reconstructs modulated token representations for downstream aggregation.
AI.result: FLaG achieves the best macro-Spearman correlation, RMSE, and Recall@50 across four AMP backbone-species settings, highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, and best mean results on five of seven language metrics (mean pooling remains best on STSBenchmark). Mechanistic analyses show low-frequency prediction sensitivity across most encoder layers, increased high-frequency sensitivity in the final layer, and peptide-specific positional responses.
AI.conclusion: FLaG provides a transferable frequency-domain aggregation bias across protein, visual, and textual representations, with performance gains that depend on the backbone and downstream task.

title: Score-Based Generative Data Assimilation for Integrating Aggregated Surveillance Data into Agent-Based Models in Epidemic Tracking
summary: Reliable epidemic monitoring often requires inferring regional infection burden and transmission heterogeneity from noisy, spatially aggregated, and potentially sparse surveillance data. Agent-based models (ABMs) are attractive for this task because they represent individual behavior, contact heterogeneity, and localized interventions, but these same features make them difficult to calibrate online. We develop a generative AI-based data-assimilation (GenDA) framework for partially observed epidemic ABMs that estimates both the epidemic state and a heterogeneous parameter field while respecting the gap between observable macrostates and latent agent-level microstates. GenDA combines a training-free, score-based generative update for macrostate correction with a direct parameter update based on macrostate discrepancies, followed by a macro-micro reassignment step that restores consistency with the ABM. In controlled and geographically explicit synthetic experiments, the framework recovers regional epidemic burden, dominant hotspot structures, and effective transmission heterogeneity from aggregated observations, while improving post-assimilation forecasts relative to state-only assimilation.

AI.tldr: A generative AI-based data-assimilation (GenDA) framework is proposed to calibrate partially observed epidemic agent-based models, estimating both epidemic state and heterogeneous parameter fields from noisy, spatially aggregated surveillance data.
AI.motivation: Epidemic monitoring requires inferring regional infection burden and transmission heterogeneity from noisy, aggregated, sparse surveillance data. While agent-based models (ABMs) can represent realistic epidemic dynamics, their individual-level complexity makes online calibration difficult.
AI.method: GenDA combines a training-free, score-based generative update for macrostate correction, a direct parameter update based on macrostate discrepancies, and a macro-micro reassignment step to restore consistency with the ABM, bridging the gap between observable macrostates and latent agent-level microstates.
AI.result: In controlled and geographically explicit synthetic experiments, GenDA recovers regional epidemic burden, dominant hotspot structures, and effective transmission heterogeneity from aggregated observations, while improving post-assimilation forecasts compared to state-only assimilation.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that jointly assimilating both state and heterogeneous parameters from aggregated data improves epidemic forecasting and situational awareness for complex ABMs.
